# Figure 4: High, asymmetric valency boosts multispecific selectivity beyond single-receptor targeting

::: {#fig-figure-4 layout-ncol="2"}
{{< embed /figures/scanning_analyses/scan_jaccard_similarity.qmd#fig-jaccard-valency >}}

{{< embed /figures/scanning_analyses/scan_top_hits_1Dvs2D.qmd#fig-top-hits-1d-2d-highval >}}

High, asymmetric valency boosts multispecific selectivity beyond single-receptor targeting. **(a)** Agreement (Jaccard index) between the top-ranked receptor pairs of selectivity scans run at different valencies, across target cell types and top-N thresholds; low overlap indicates that the optimal multi-receptor hits shift as valency changes. **(b)** High, asymmetric valency (mixed tetravalent): maximum achievable selectivity from a single target receptor (1D) versus the best receptor pair (2D), per target cell type; unlike the low-valency case, many cell types rise well above the diagonal, so the best receptor pair substantially beats the best single receptor (blue = pairing helps, 2D ≥ 1D; red = 2D < 1D).
:::

* Intuition tells us that some changes in binding model optimization problems may lead to multi-receptor prioritization:
  + Different signal receptors
  +	Higher valency
  +	Asymmetric target ligand valencies
* Top hits are consistent across signal receptor definitions (generic or specific) (@suppfig-jaccard-signal)
* Top hits are variable with changes in valency (magnitude and asymmetry) (@fig-jaccard-valency)
* Increasing valency increases the utility of optimal multispecificity (@fig-top-hits-1d-2d-highval, @suppfig-top-hits-gain-highval)
* Asymmetric valency of paired targets further improves multi-receptor selectivity?
